terms.gloss: (asks a question) is it …? do you …?
terms.grammar: enclitic particle, joined to the first word of the question
evidence: Catull. 9.3: vēnistīne domum ad tuōs penātēs?
terms.comment: The open question, expecting neither yes nor no; it goes on the word asked about, most often the verb (Lewis & Short). In speech it is worn down to -n'. The answer repeats the verb, Valeō (see “yes”); in speech the particle may be left off and the voice alone ask (tū hīc erās?, Ter. Ad. 901).

terms.grammar: adverb, at the head of the question
evidence: Plaut. Amph. 406: nōnne ego nunc stō ante aedēs nostrās?
Cic. N. D. 3.89: nōnne animadvertis? (Lewis & Short)

terms.grammar: adverb, at the head of the question
evidence: Ter. Ph. 846: Num tū intellegis hīc quid narret?
terms.comment: Numquid vīs?, “anything else?”, is the everyday way of taking leave (Lewis & Short). In an indirect question num is “whether”.

terms.gloss: or …?; (opening a question) so …? can it be that …?
evidence: Ter. Hec. 346: Quid ais? an vēnit Pamphilus?
terms.comment: Introduces the second half of a double question: utrum … an, -ne … an, “is it this or that?” (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Valēn'? valuistīn'? — Valeō, et valuī rēctius.
phrases.english: Are you well? Have you been well? — I’m well, and I’ve been better.

phrases.latin: vēnistīne domum ad tuōs penātēs frātrēsque ūnanimōs anumque mātrem?
phrases.english: have you come home to your own hearth, your loving brothers and your old mother?
Tell me, did you run away? — Yes, mistress, I did.

phrases.latin: Num tū intellegis hīc quid narret? — Num tū? — Nihil. — Tantundem ego.
phrases.english: You don’t understand what he’s saying, do you? — Do you? — Not a word. — Nor I.

phrases.latin: nōnne ego nunc stō ante aedēs nostrās? nōn mī est lanterna in manū?
phrases.english: Am I not standing in front of our house? Haven’t I a lantern in my hand?

phrases.latin: Quid agitur, Aeschine? — Ehem, pater mī, tū hīc erās?
phrases.english: How are things, Aeschinus? — Oh, father, you were here?
